A **Hopf algebra over $k$** is a bialgebra $H$ together with a $k$-linear map $S:H\to H$, called its **antipode**, such that

$$S*\mathrm{id}_H=u\varepsilon=\mathrm{id}_H*S,$$

where $*$ is the convolution product on $\operatorname{Hom}_k(H,H)$, $u:k\to H$ is the unit, and $\varepsilon:H\to k$ is the counit. Equivalently, $m(S\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta=u\varepsilon=m(\mathrm{id}\otimes S)\Delta$. Thus $S$ is the two-sided inverse of $\mathrm{id}_H$ in the convolution algebra. This definition imposes no compositional bijectivity condition on $S$.

For a finite-dimensional unital associative $k$-algebra $A$, the full dual $A^*$ is a coalgebra under the transpose of multiplication and unit. For every coalgebra $C$, the full dual $C^*$ is a unital associative algebra under convolution. These dualizations reverse algebra and coalgebra maps. Restricted to finite-dimensional objects, the two contravariant dualizations are inverse equivalences via the canonical evaluation maps $A\to A^{**}$ and $C\to C^{**}$. The finite-dimensionality hypothesis in the algebra-to-coalgebra direction is on $A$ itself, not merely on a module over $A$.

Let $V,W$ be finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces.

1. The bilinear map $V^*\times W^*\to(V\otimes W)^*$, $(f,g)\mapsto[v\otimes w\mapsto f(v)g(w)]$, induces an isomorphism $V^*\otimes W^*\to(V\otimes W)^*$. For ordered bases $(v_1,\dots,v_m)$ of $V$, $(w_1,\dots,w_n)$ of $W$ with dual bases $(v_i^*)$, $(w_j^*)$, the image of $v_i^*\otimes w_j^*$ is the dual basis vector of $v_i\otimes w_j$ in the product basis of $V\otimes W$.
2. For every ordered basis $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ of $V$ the element $\sum_{i=1}^nv_i^*\otimes v_i\in V^*\otimes V$ is independent of the basis and corresponds to $\mathrm{id}_V$ under the isomorphism $V^*\otimes V\to\operatorname{Hom}(V,V)$, $f\otimes v\mapsto[x\mapsto f(x)v]$ ([[thm-hom-from-a-finite-dimensional-space-as-a-tensor-product]]). Its image under $\sigma_{V^*,V}$ is the corresponding element $\sum_iv_i\otimes v_i^*$ of $V\otimes V^*$.
3. The evaluation $\mathrm{ev}:V^*\otimes V\to k$, $f\otimes v\mapsto f(v)$, and the coevaluation $\mathrm{coev}:k\to V\otimes V^*$, $1\mapsto\sum_iv_i\otimes v_i^*$, are independent of the basis and satisfy $(\mathrm{id}_V\otimes\mathrm{ev})\circ\alpha_{V,V^*,V}\circ(\mathrm{coev}\otimes\mathrm{id}_V)=\mathrm{id}_V$ and $(\mathrm{ev}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{V^*})\circ\alpha^{-1}_{V^*,V,V^*}\circ(\mathrm{id}_{V^*}\otimes\mathrm{coev})=\mathrm{id}_{V^*}$, the unit isomorphisms $k\otimes V\cong V$, $V\otimes k\cong V$ being understood.

Fix a field $k$. A **bialgebra over $k$** is a $k$-vector space $H$ with a unital associative $k$-algebra structure $(m,u)$ and a counital coassociative $k$-coalgebra structure $(\Delta,\varepsilon)$ in the sense of [[def-hh-coalgebra-and-coalgebra-map]], where $m:H\otimes H\to H$, $u:k\to H$, $\Delta:H\to H\otimes H$, and $\varepsilon:H\to k$. Explicitly, the algebra equations are $m(m\otimes\mathrm{id})=m(\mathrm{id}\otimes m)$ and $m(u\otimes\mathrm{id})=\mathrm{id}=m(\mathrm{id}\otimes u)$ under the canonical identifications; the coalgebra equations are those of [[def-hh-coalgebra-and-coalgebra-map]].

Require $\Delta:H\to H\otimes H$ and $\varepsilon:H\to k$ to be unital algebra homomorphisms. The algebra on $H\otimes H$ is the one with $(a\otimes b)(c\otimes d)=ac\otimes bd$ and unit $1_H\otimes1_H$; the algebra on $k$ is its field algebra. A **bialgebra map** $f:H\to K$ is a $k$-linear map preserving multiplication, unit, comultiplication, and counit: $f m_H=m_K(f\otimes f)$, $fu_H=u_K$, $\Delta_Kf=(f\otimes f)\Delta_H$, and $\varepsilon_Kf=\varepsilon_H$.

For a fixed comultiplication $\Delta:C\to C\otimes C$, there is at most one counit. Also, Sweedler notation records a finite tensor sum, not a list of canonical summands: every contraction written from that notation must be the value of a well-defined linear map on the tensor.

derivations.claim: Since $H$ is finite-dimensional, [F3] identifies $(H\otimes H)^*$ with $H^*\otimes H^*$; thus for each $\phi\in H^*$, the transpose $m^*(\phi)$ is a tensor $\sum_i\phi_i\otimes\psi_i$ characterized by $\phi(ab)=\sum_i\phi_i(a)\psi_i(b)$. The same finite tensor duality for $H\otimes H$ permits transposing every structural identity in [F1] and [F2].

The convolution product on $H^*$ is associative: evaluating $(\phi\psi)\theta$ and $\phi(\psi\theta)$ on $h$ gives respectively $\sum\phi(h_1)\psi(h_2)\theta(h_3)$ through the two iterated coproducts of $H$, which agree by coassociativity; the counit identities make $\varepsilon$ its left and right unit.

The coproduct $m^*$ on $H^*$ is coassociative because evaluating $(m^*\otimes\mathrm{id})m^*(\phi)$ and $(\mathrm{id}\otimes m^*)m^*(\phi)$ on $a\otimes b\otimes c$ gives $\phi((ab)c)$ and $\phi(a(bc))$, equal by associativity of $H$; evaluation at $1_H$ is a two-sided counit by $1_Ha=a=a1_H$.

The coproduct on $H^*$ preserves convolution products: for $\phi,\psi\in H^*$ and $a,b\in H$, $\Delta_{H^*}(\phi\psi)(a\otimes b) =(\phi\psi)(ab) =\sum \phi(a_1b_1)\psi(a_2b_2) =\bigl(\Delta_{H^*}(\phi)\Delta_{H^*}(\psi)\bigr)(a\otimes b),$ where the second equality uses that $\Delta_H$ is an algebra map. Finite tensor duality makes equality on all $a\otimes b$ equality of tensors.

The unit $\varepsilon_H$ is group-like for $\Delta_{H^*}$, since $\varepsilon_H(ab)=\varepsilon_H(a)\varepsilon_H(b)$; the counit $\phi\mapsto\phi(1_H)$ preserves convolution products because $\Delta_H(1_H)=1_H\otimes1_H$. Thus the maps in the Statement make $H^*$ a bialgebra.

Define $S^*(\phi)=\phi\circ S$. If $\Delta_{H^*}(\phi)=\sum_i\phi_i\otimes\psi_i$, then for $h\in H$, $\bigl(S^*(\phi_{(1)})\phi_{(2)}\bigr)(h) =\sum_{(h),i}\phi_i(S(h_1))\psi_i(h_2) =\sum_{(h)}\phi(S(h_1)h_2) =\varepsilon(h)\phi(1_H).$ The last equality is the left antipode equation in [F1]; this is the left antipode equation for $S^*$ in $H^*$.

Likewise, $\bigl(\phi_{(1)}S^*(\phi_{(2)})\bigr)(h) =\sum_{(h),i}\phi_i(h_1)\psi_i(S(h_2)) =\sum_{(h)}\phi(h_1S(h_2)) =\varepsilon(h)\phi(1_H),$ using the right antipode equation in [F1]. Both convolution equations hold, so $S^*$ is an antipode on $H^*$, and no step uses $S^{-1}$.

$$S*\mathrm{id}_H=u\varepsilon=\mathrm{id}_H*S,$$

Equivalently, $m(S\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta=u\varepsilon=m(\mathrm{id}\otimes S)\Delta$. Thus $S$ is the two-sided inverse of $\mathrm{id}_H$ in the convolution algebra. This definition imposes no compositional bijectivity condition on $S$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $S$ a set. There is a unital associative $R$-algebra $R\langle S\rangle$, the **free associative $R$-algebra on $S$**, whose underlying $R$-module is free on the set of finite words in $S$ (including the empty word), with product given on words by concatenation and extended $R$-bilinearly.

1. **Universal property.** For every $R$-algebra $A$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and every map $S\to A$ there is a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $R\langle S\rangle\to A$ extending it. When $R=k$ is a field and $S$ indexes a basis of a vector space $V$, $R\langle S\rangle$ reproduces the published tensor algebra $T(V)$ ([[def-tensor-algebra-of-a-vector-space]], [[thm-universal-property-of-the-tensor-algebra]]).
2. **Two-sided ideal description.** For $E\subseteq R\langle S\rangle$ the two-sided ideal $(E)$ ([[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]]) is the set of finite sums $\sum_sa_se_sb_s$ with $a_s,b_s\in R\langle S\rangle$ and $e_s\in E$.
3. **Quotient universal property.** If $\varphi:R\langle S\rangle\to A$ is an $R$-algebra homomorphism killing $E$, then $\varphi$ factors uniquely through the quotient $R\langle S\rangle/(E)$ ([[thm-quotient-ring-universal-property]]); the quotient is the presented $R$-algebra with generators $S$ and relations $E$.

Fix the following conventions, used on this page and by the later Hopf and Hecke pages.

- $k$ is a field ([[def-field]]) and every vector space is a $k$-vector space ([[def-vector-space]]); $\otimes$ means $\otimes_k$.
- $V\otimes W$ is the tensor product of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]], with the $k$-vector-space structure of [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and unit and universal property as in [[thm-universal-property-of-module-tensor-products]]. Every element of $V\otimes W$ is a finite sum of elementary tensors $v\otimes w$.
- Tensor powers are left-associated: $V^{\otimes 0}:=k$, $V^{\otimes 1}:=V$ and $V^{\otimes n}:=(V^{\otimes(n-1)})\otimes V$ for $n\ge2$. The empty tensor $k$ is identified with the tensor unit through the isomorphisms of [[thm-unit-isomorphisms-for-module-tensor-products]].
- For an algebra $A$ over a commutative ring ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) the opposite algebra $A^{\mathrm{op}}$ has the same underlying set and structure map and product $a\cdot b:=ba$ ([[def-opposite-ring]]).
- Finite sums $\sum_{i\in I}x_i$ follow [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]; an empty sum is $0$.

Parentheses in iterated tensor products may be dropped only after [[lem-hh-tensor-coherence-on-elementary-tensors]] has been proved.

Let $k$ be a field and let $L,M,N,X$ be $k$-vector spaces. Write $\alpha_{A,B,C}:(A\otimes B)\otimes C\to A\otimes(B\otimes C)$ for the associators of [[thm-symmetry-and-associativity-over-a-commutative-ring]], $\sigma_{A,B}$ for its symmetries, and $\lambda,\rho$ for the unit isomorphisms of [[thm-unit-isomorphisms-for-module-tensor-products]].

1. **Naturality.** $\alpha$ and $\sigma$ are natural in all variables: for linear maps the usual squares commute; the unit isomorphisms are natural as well.
2. **Pentagon.** $(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\alpha_{M,N,X})\circ\alpha_{L,M\otimes N,X}\circ(\alpha_{L,M,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_X)=\alpha_{L,M,N\otimes X}\circ\alpha_{L\otimes M,N,X}$ as maps $((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\otimes X\to L\otimes(M\otimes(N\otimes X))$.
3. **Unit triangle.** $(\mathrm{id}_M\otimes\lambda_N)\circ\alpha_{M,k,N}=\rho_M\otimes\mathrm{id}_N$ as maps $(M\otimes k)\otimes N\to M\otimes N$.
4. **First symmetry hexagon.** $\alpha_{L,N,M}\circ(\sigma_{N,L}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{N,L,M}\circ\sigma_{L\otimes M,N}=(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\sigma_{M,N})\circ\alpha_{L,M,N}$ as maps $((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\to L\otimes(N\otimes M)$.
5. **Second symmetry hexagon.** $\alpha^{-1}_{N,L,M}\circ\sigma_{L\otimes M,N}\circ\alpha^{-1}_{L,M,N}=(\sigma_{L,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{L,N,M}\circ(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\sigma_{M,N})$ as maps $L\otimes(M\otimes N)\to(N\otimes L)\otimes M$.

All five identities are equalities of $k$-linear maps between iterated tensor products.

For a fixed comultiplication $\Delta:C\to C\otimes C$, there is at most one counit. Also, Sweedler notation records a finite tensor sum, not a list of canonical summands: every contraction written from that notation must be the value of a well-defined linear map on the tensor.

derivations.claim: Let $T$ be the vector space with basis $e_{i,j}$, $i\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, $0\le j<N$, and extend bilinearly the rule $e_{i,j}e_{a,b}=\zeta^{-aj}e_{i+a,j+b}$ when $j+b<N$, and $0$ otherwise. For a triple of basis elements, if $j+b+d\ge N$, both parenthesizations vanish: if an intermediate degree reaches $N$ it is truncated, and otherwise the final multiplication truncates. If $j+b+d<N$, the scalar in $(e_{i,j}e_{a,b})e_{c,d}$ is $\zeta^{-aj-c(j+b)}$, while the scalar in $e_{i,j}(e_{a,b}e_{c,d})$ is $\zeta^{-cb-(a+c)j}$; these exponents are equal, and both outputs are $e_{i+a+c,j+b+d}$. Hence multiplication is associative by bilinearity, and $e_{0,0}$ is its two-sided unit.

Put $g=e_{1,0}$ and $x=e_{0,1}$. The formula gives $g^N=e_{0,0}$, $x^N=0$, $gx=e_{1,1}$, and $xg=\zeta^{-1}e_{1,1}$, so $gx=\zeta xg$. Thus the relations define a surjective algebra map from the presented quotient $Q=k\langle g,x\rangle/(g^N-1,x^N,gx-\zeta xg)$ to $T$, since each $e_{i,j}$ is the image of $g^i x^j$, by [F2].

In $Q$, the relation $xg=\zeta^{-1}gx$ moves every $g$ to the left of every $x$; reducing $g$-powers modulo $N$ and setting any $x$-power at least $N$ to zero shows that the $N^2$ words $g^i x^j$, $0\le i,j<N$, span $Q$. Their images in $T$ are its distinct basis vectors $e_{i,j}$, hence are linearly independent in $Q$ as well. Therefore $Q\to T$ is an isomorphism and the claimed PBW basis is valid.

Define $\Delta$ on the free algebra by the stated generator images. They preserve the relations: $\Delta(g)^N=1$, and with $A=1\otimes x$, $B=x\otimes g$ one has $BA=\zeta AB$ and $\Delta(x)=A+B$. If $(A+B)^n=\sum_{r=0}^n C_{n,r}A^{n-r}B^r$, then $C_{0,0}=1$ and $C_{n+1,r}=\zeta^rC_{n,r}+C_{n,r-1}$, since $B^rA=\zeta^rAB^r$. For $0\le n<N$ and $0\le r\le n$, the recurrence gives $C_{n,r}=\prod_{s=1}^r(1-\zeta^{n-r+s})/(1-\zeta^s)$: for $1\le r\le n$, set $P=\prod_{s=1}^{r-1}(1-\zeta^{n-r+1+s})$ and $D=\prod_{s=1}^r(1-\zeta^s)$; then $C_{n,r}=P(1-\zeta^{n-r+1})/D$ and $C_{n,r-1}=P(1-\zeta^r)/D$, so $\zeta^rC_{n,r}+C_{n,r-1}=P(1-\zeta^{n+1})/D=C_{n+1,r}$. For $n=N$ and $0<r<N$, the same formula has nonzero denominator factors and a numerator factor $1-\zeta^N=0$; hence $(A+B)^N=A^N+B^N=0$. Also $\Delta(g)\Delta(x)=g\otimes gx+gx\otimes g^2=\zeta(g\otimes xg+xg\otimes g^2)=\zeta\Delta(x)\Delta(g)$, so $\Delta(gx-\zeta xg)=0$, and $\Delta$ descends to $Q$.

Extend $S$ as an anti-algebra map from the free algebra using $S(g)=g^{-1}$ and $S(x)=-xg^{-1}$. The relation ideal is killed: $S(g^N-1)=g^{-N}-1=0$; reordering with $g^{-1}x=\zeta^{-1}xg^{-1}$ shows $S(x^N)=(-xg^{-1})^N$ is a scalar multiple of $x^Ng^{-N}=0$; and $S(gx-\zeta xg)=S(x)S(g)-\zeta S(g)S(x)=-xg^{-2}+\zeta g^{-1}xg^{-1}=0$. Thus $S$ descends to $Q$.

The assignment $\varepsilon(g)=1,\varepsilon(x)=0$ kills $g^N-1$, $x^N$, and $gx-\zeta xg$, so it descends to an algebra map $Q\to k$. Coassociativity holds on $g$ immediately; on $x$, both iterates equal $1\otimes1\otimes x+1\otimes x\otimes g+x\otimes g\otimes g$. The two counit equations hold on $g,x$ by the given values. These maps are algebra maps, and the presented algebra is generated by $g,x$, so the identities extend to all of $Q$.

On $g$, both $m(S\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta$ and $m(\mathrm{id}\otimes S)\Delta$ give $1=\varepsilon(g)1$. On $x$, the left product is $x+(-xg^{-1})g=0$, and the right product is $-xg^{-1}+xg^{-1}=0=\varepsilon(x)1$. For products $ab$ of elements on which both identities hold, anti-multiplicativity of $S$ and multiplicativity of $\Delta$ give $\sum S(a_1b_1)a_2b_2=\sum S(b_1)(S(a_1)a_2)b_2=\varepsilon(a)\varepsilon(b)1$, and $\sum a_1b_1S(a_2b_2)=\sum a_1(b_1S(b_2))S(a_2)=\varepsilon(a)\varepsilon(b)1$. Induction on word length and linearity extend both antipode equations to all of $Q$. Thus the given maps make $Q$ a Hopf algebra, with the interface of [F1].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $k$ be a field and let $H=(H,m,u,\Delta,\varepsilon,S)$ be a Hopf $k$-algebra as in [[def-hh-hopf-algebra-and-antipode]], with $S$ satisfying both convolution antipode equations. A **subbialgebra** of $H$ is a $k$-subspace $K\subseteq H$ equipped with a bialgebra structure as in [[def-hh-bialgebra-and-bialgebra-map]] for which the inclusion $K\hookrightarrow H$ is a bialgebra map. A **Hopf subalgebra** is a subbialgebra $K$ with $S(K)\subseteq K$. Under AC, meaning every family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the tensor-injection lemma [[lem-hh-tensor-injections-quotients-and-kernels-over-a-field]] identifies $K\otimes K$ with its image in $H\otimes H$; in that shorthand, the subbialgebra condition says exactly that $K$ is a unital subalgebra, $\Delta_H(K)\subseteq K\otimes K$, and the counit is restricted from $H$.

A **Hopf ideal** is a two-sided ideal in the sense of [[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]], $I\trianglelefteq H$, satisfying $\varepsilon_H(I)=0$, $S(I)\subseteq I$, and the coideal condition from [[def-hh-subcoalgebras-coideals-and-quotient-coalgebras]]: $\Delta_H(I)\subseteq\operatorname{im}(I\otimes H\to H\otimes H)+\operatorname{im}(H\otimes I\to H\otimes H)$. Under AC, the tensor-injection lemma identifies these tensor products with subspaces of $H\otimes H$, giving the usual shorthand $\Delta_H(I)\subseteq I\otimes H+H\otimes I$. The two-sided ideal condition gives the unital quotient algebra $H/I$; $\varepsilon_H(I)=0$ makes its counit descend, and the remaining conditions are precisely those needed for the coproduct and antipode to descend. A subbialgebra is not called a Hopf subalgebra unless the antipode restricts to it.

A ring homomorphism whose kernel contains a two-sided ideal factors uniquely through the quotient ring.

If $I\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}R$, $f:R\to S$ is a ring homomorphism, and
$I\subseteq\ker f$, there is a unique ring homomorphism $\bar f:R/I\to S$ such
that $\bar f(r+I)=f(r)$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $A,B$ be $R$-algebras. The $R$-module $A\otimes_RB$ has a unique $R$-algebra structure satisfying

$$(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')=aa'\otimes bb'$$

and

$$1_{A\otimes_RB}=1_A\otimes1_B,\qquad r\longmapsto r(1_A\otimes1_B).$$

If $A$ and $B$ are commutative, then $A\otimes_RB$ is commutative.

Fix a field $k$. A **bialgebra over $k$** is a $k$-vector space $H$ with a unital associative $k$-algebra structure $(m,u)$ and a counital coassociative $k$-coalgebra structure $(\Delta,\varepsilon)$ in the sense of [[def-hh-coalgebra-and-coalgebra-map]], where $m:H\otimes H\to H$, $u:k\to H$, $\Delta:H\to H\otimes H$, and $\varepsilon:H\to k$. Explicitly, the algebra equations are $m(m\otimes\mathrm{id})=m(\mathrm{id}\otimes m)$ and $m(u\otimes\mathrm{id})=\mathrm{id}=m(\mathrm{id}\otimes u)$ under the canonical identifications; the coalgebra equations are those of [[def-hh-coalgebra-and-coalgebra-map]].

Require $\Delta:H\to H\otimes H$ and $\varepsilon:H\to k$ to be unital algebra homomorphisms. The algebra on $H\otimes H$ is the one with $(a\otimes b)(c\otimes d)=ac\otimes bd$ and unit $1_H\otimes1_H$; the algebra on $k$ is its field algebra. A **bialgebra map** $f:H\to K$ is a $k$-linear map preserving multiplication, unit, comultiplication, and counit: $f m_H=m_K(f\otimes f)$, $fu_H=u_K$, $\Delta_Kf=(f\otimes f)\Delta_H$, and $\varepsilon_Kf=\varepsilon_H$.

Let $k$ be a field, let $C$ be a $k$-coalgebra with comultiplication $\Delta_C$ and counit $\varepsilon_C$, and let $A$ be a unital associative $k$-algebra with multiplication $m_A$ and unit map $u_A$. On the $k$-vector space $\operatorname{Hom}_k(C,A)$ define

$$f*g:=m_A(f\otimes g)\Delta_C. $$

This is a well-defined associative multiplication with two-sided unit $u_A\varepsilon_C$. The assertion holds without a finite-dimensionality assumption on either $C$ or $A$.

Let $H$ be a Hopf algebra over a field $k$, with antipode $S$, multiplication $m$, unit $u$, comultiplication $\Delta$, and counit $\varepsilon$. Then $S$ is unique, $S(1)=1$, and $\varepsilon\circ S=\varepsilon$. Moreover, for all $a,b\in H$,

$$S(ab)=S(b)S(a),\qquad \Delta(S(h))=(S\otimes S)\tau\Delta(h)\quad(h\in H),$$

where $\tau(x\otimes y)=y\otimes x$ is the tensor flip. In particular, these are consequences of the convolution-inverse definition; they are not extra axioms.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be a field, let $f:V\to V'$ be an injective linear map and let $W$ be a $k$-vector space. Then $f\otimes\mathrm{id}_W:V\otimes W\to V'\otimes W$ is injective. Moreover, if $U\subseteq V$ and $Z\subseteq W$ are subspaces and $p:V\to V/U$, $q:W\to W/Z$ are the quotient maps, then, viewing $U\otimes W$ and $V\otimes Z$ as subspaces of $V\otimes W$ through the injections of the first part and the inclusions $U\subseteq V$, $Z\subseteq W$,
$$\ker(p\otimes q)=U\otimes W+V\otimes Z .$$

Fix the following conventions, used on this page and by the later Hopf and Hecke pages.

- $k$ is a field ([[def-field]]) and every vector space is a $k$-vector space ([[def-vector-space]]); $\otimes$ means $\otimes_k$.
- $V\otimes W$ is the tensor product of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]], with the $k$-vector-space structure of [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and unit and universal property as in [[thm-universal-property-of-module-tensor-products]]. Every element of $V\otimes W$ is a finite sum of elementary tensors $v\otimes w$.
- Tensor powers are left-associated: $V^{\otimes 0}:=k$, $V^{\otimes 1}:=V$ and $V^{\otimes n}:=(V^{\otimes(n-1)})\otimes V$ for $n\ge2$. The empty tensor $k$ is identified with the tensor unit through the isomorphisms of [[thm-unit-isomorphisms-for-module-tensor-products]].
- For an algebra $A$ over a commutative ring ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) the opposite algebra $A^{\mathrm{op}}$ has the same underlying set and structure map and product $a\cdot b:=ba$ ([[def-opposite-ring]]).
- Finite sums $\sum_{i\in I}x_i$ follow [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]; an empty sum is $0$.

Parentheses in iterated tensor products may be dropped only after [[lem-hh-tensor-coherence-on-elementary-tensors]] has been proved.

Let $k$ be a field and let $L,M,N,X$ be $k$-vector spaces. Write $\alpha_{A,B,C}:(A\otimes B)\otimes C\to A\otimes(B\otimes C)$ for the associators of [[thm-symmetry-and-associativity-over-a-commutative-ring]], $\sigma_{A,B}$ for its symmetries, and $\lambda,\rho$ for the unit isomorphisms of [[thm-unit-isomorphisms-for-module-tensor-products]].

1. **Naturality.** $\alpha$ and $\sigma$ are natural in all variables: for linear maps the usual squares commute; the unit isomorphisms are natural as well.
2. **Pentagon.** $(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\alpha_{M,N,X})\circ\alpha_{L,M\otimes N,X}\circ(\alpha_{L,M,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_X)=\alpha_{L,M,N\otimes X}\circ\alpha_{L\otimes M,N,X}$ as maps $((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\otimes X\to L\otimes(M\otimes(N\otimes X))$.
3. **Unit triangle.** $(\mathrm{id}_M\otimes\lambda_N)\circ\alpha_{M,k,N}=\rho_M\otimes\mathrm{id}_N$ as maps $(M\otimes k)\otimes N\to M\otimes N$.
4. **First symmetry hexagon.** $\alpha_{L,N,M}\circ(\sigma_{N,L}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{N,L,M}\circ\sigma_{L\otimes M,N}=(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\sigma_{M,N})\circ\alpha_{L,M,N}$ as maps $((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\to L\otimes(N\otimes M)$.
5. **Second symmetry hexagon.** $\alpha^{-1}_{N,L,M}\circ\sigma_{L\otimes M,N}\circ\alpha^{-1}_{L,M,N}=(\sigma_{L,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{L,N,M}\circ(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\sigma_{M,N})$ as maps $L\otimes(M\otimes N)\to(N\otimes L)\otimes M$.

All five identities are equalities of $k$-linear maps between iterated tensor products.

A **Hopf algebra over $k$** is a bialgebra $H$ together with a $k$-linear map $S:H\to H$, called its **antipode**, such that

$$S*\mathrm{id}_H=u\varepsilon=\mathrm{id}_H*S,$$

where $*$ is the convolution product on $\operatorname{Hom}_k(H,H)$, $u:k\to H$ is the unit, and $\varepsilon:H\to k$ is the counit. Equivalently, $m(S\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta=u\varepsilon=m(\mathrm{id}\otimes S)\Delta$. Thus $S$ is the two-sided inverse of $\mathrm{id}_H$ in the convolution algebra. This definition imposes no compositional bijectivity condition on $S$.

For a fixed comultiplication $\Delta:C\to C\otimes C$, there is at most one counit. Also, Sweedler notation records a finite tensor sum, not a list of canonical summands: every contraction written from that notation must be the value of a well-defined linear map on the tensor.

derivations.claim: The quotient multiplication $(h+I)(h'+I)=hh'+I$ and unit $1_H+I$ are well-defined because $I$ is a two-sided ideal; [F2] gives the unique algebra map $q_I:H\to H/I$.

Define $\overline{\Delta}(h+I):=(q_I\otimes q_I)\Delta_H(h)$. If $h-h'\in I$, then $\Delta(h-h')$ lies in the sum of the two tensor images in [F1], and $q_I\otimes q_I$ kills both, so the formula is independent of the representative. Define $\overline{\varepsilon}(h+I):=\varepsilon_H(h)$, which is well-defined by [F1]. These formulas construct linear maps on the quotient directly.
Define $\overline S(h+I):=S_H(h)+I$. It is well-defined because $S_H(I)\subseteq I$ by [F1].

For any bialgebra map $f:H\to K$, the maps $S_Kf$ and $fS_H$ are both two-sided convolution inverses of $f$. Indeed, $(S_Kf)*f=m_K(S_K\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta_Kf=u_K\varepsilon_H$ and $f*(S_Kf)=m_K(\mathrm{id}\otimes S_K)\Delta_Kf=u_K\varepsilon_H$, using that $f$ is a coalgebra map and both antipode identities in $K$; also $(fS_H)*f=fm_H(S_H\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta_H=u_K\varepsilon_H$ and $f*(fS_H)=fm_H(\mathrm{id}\otimes S_H)\Delta_H=u_K\varepsilon_H$, using multiplicativity of $f$ and both antipode identities in $H$. By uniqueness of two-sided inverses in the associative convolution algebra [F5, F6], $S_Kf=fS_H$.
For a Hopf map $f:H\to K$, $J:=\ker f$ is a two-sided ideal and $\varepsilon_H(J)=0$, since $f$ preserves multiplication, unit, and counit by [F4].

By [F2], $f=\widetilde f q_J$ for a linear map $\widetilde f:H/J\to K$, and $\widetilde f$ is injective because $\widetilde f(h+J)=f(h)=0$ implies $h\in J$. By [F7], $\widetilde f\otimes\widetilde f$ is injective and $\ker(q_J\otimes q_J)=J\otimes H+H\otimes J$; hence $\ker(f\otimes f)=J\otimes H+H\otimes J$. For $j\in J$, $(f\otimes f)\Delta_H(j)=\Delta_K(f(j))=0$ by [F4], so $\Delta_H(j)\in J\otimes H+H\otimes J$.

Give $H\otimes K$ the algebra structure from [F3]. Define $\Delta_T(h\otimes k)=\sum(h_1\otimes k_1)\otimes(h_2\otimes k_2)$, $\varepsilon_T(h\otimes k)=\varepsilon_H(h)\varepsilon_K(k)$, and $S_T(h\otimes k)=S_H(h)\otimes S_K(k)$; these are the displayed maps with the middle factors flipped.

For pure tensors, multiplicativity of the coproduct follows from $\Delta_T((h\otimes k)(h'\otimes k'))=\sum(h_1h'_1\otimes k_1k'_1)\otimes(h_2h'_2\otimes k_2k'_2)=\Delta_T(h\otimes k)\Delta_T(h'\otimes k')$, using that $\Delta_H,\Delta_K$ are algebra maps and the tensor-product multiplication [F3, F4]. Unit preservation follows from $\Delta_H(1)=1\otimes1$ and $\Delta_K(1)=1\otimes1$. Also $\varepsilon_T((h\otimes k)(h'\otimes k'))=\varepsilon_H(hh')\varepsilon_K(kk')=\varepsilon_T(h\otimes k)\varepsilon_T(h'\otimes k')$, and $\varepsilon_T(1_H\otimes1_K)=1$, since both counits are unital algebra maps by [F4]. These equations extend linearly from pure tensors.

For $h,h'\in H$, $\overline\Delta((h+I)(h'+I))=(q_I\otimes q_I)\Delta_H(hh')=(q_I\otimes q_I)(\Delta_H(h)\Delta_H(h'))=\overline\Delta(h+I)\overline\Delta(h'+I)$, using that $\Delta_H$ is an algebra map and [F3] gives the tensor-product algebra. Also $\overline\Delta(1+I)=(1+I)\otimes(1+I)$, $\overline\varepsilon((h+I)(h'+I))=\varepsilon_H(h)\varepsilon_H(h')$, and $\overline\varepsilon(1+I)=1$, by [F4]. Coassociativity follows since the two composites on $h+I$ are respectively $(q_I\otimes q_I\otimes q_I)(\Delta_H\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta_H(h)$ and $(q_I\otimes q_I\otimes q_I)(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta_H)\Delta_H(h)$, equal by coassociativity in $H$; the associators and tensor maps are natural by [F8]. The left counit composite on $h+I$ is $\sum\overline\varepsilon(h_1+I)(h_2+I)=\sum\varepsilon_H(h_1)(h_2+I)=h+I$, and the right composite is $\sum(h_1+I)\varepsilon_H(h_2)=h+I$, by the two counit equations in $H$. For the left antipode equation, its value on $h+I$ is $\sum (S_H(h_1)+I)(h_2+I)=q_I(\sum S_H(h_1)h_2)=\varepsilon_H(h)(1+I)$; the right equation is $\sum(h_1+I)(S_H(h_2)+I)=q_I(\sum h_1S_H(h_2))=\varepsilon_H(h)(1+I)$. Thus these maps make $H/I$ a Hopf algebra. Since $q_I$ is surjective and $q_I\otimes q_I$ is surjective (each elementary tensor of cosets has representatives and such tensors span), the quotient algebra and coalgebra maps are forced by $q_I$; the antipode is unique as a two-sided convolution inverse by [F5, F6].

If a Hopf map $f:H\to K$ kills $I$, [F2] gives a unique algebra map $\bar f:H/I\to K$ with $\bar f q_I=f$. Precomposing the coalgebra-map equation with $q_I$ gives $(\bar f\otimes\bar f)\overline\Delta q_I=(f\otimes f)\Delta_H=\Delta_K f=\Delta_K\bar f q_I$; surjectivity of $q_I$ proves the equation on $H/I$. Counit preservation follows from $\bar f q_I=f$ and surjectivity of $q_I$. For antipodes, $\bar f\overline S q_I=\bar f q_I S_H=fS_H=S_Kf=S_K\bar f q_I$ by step 1.4; surjectivity of $q_I$ proves $\bar f\overline S=S_K\bar f$. Thus $\bar f$ is a Hopf map.
By step 1.4, $S_Kf=fS_H$. Therefore for $j\in J$, $f(S_H(j))=S_K(f(j))=S_K(0)=0$, so $S_H(J)\subseteq J$. Together with steps 1.5 and 1.6, this says $J$ is a Hopf ideal.

On $h\otimes k$, the two iterated coproducts are $\sum(h_{11}\otimes k_{11})\otimes(h_{12}\otimes k_{12})\otimes(h_2\otimes k_2)$ and $\sum(h_1\otimes k_1)\otimes(h_{21}\otimes k_{21})\otimes(h_{22}\otimes k_{22})$; they agree by coassociativity in $H,K$. Applying the left counit leg gives $\sum\varepsilon_H(h_1)\varepsilon_K(k_1)(h_2\otimes k_2)=h\otimes k$; applying the right leg gives $\sum(h_1\otimes k_1)\varepsilon_H(h_2)\varepsilon_K(k_2)=h\otimes k$, by counitality in each factor. Thus $H\otimes K$ is a bialgebra.

The left antipode product is $\sum (S_H(h_1)\otimes S_K(k_1))(h_2\otimes k_2)=\varepsilon_H(h)\varepsilon_K(k)(1_H\otimes1_K)$, and the right product is $\sum (h_1\otimes k_1)(S_H(h_2)\otimes S_K(k_2))=\varepsilon_H(h)\varepsilon_K(k)(1_H\otimes1_K)$. Each equality is the tensor product of the corresponding antipode identity in $H$ and $K$, so $S_T$ is an antipode. The quotient and tensor-product constructions use no choice; AC is used only in the kernel tensor calculation through [F7].

Let $k$ be a field ([[def-field]]) and let $A$ be a unital associative $k$-algebra ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). Its **finite dual** (also called its restricted dual) is the subset
$$
A^\circ:=\{f\in A^*: \text{there is a two-sided ideal }I\trianglelefteq A \text{ with }\dim_k(A/I)<\infty\text{ and }f(I)=0\}.
$$
Equivalently, $f\in A^\circ$ exactly when it factors through a finite-dimensional quotient algebra $A/I$. The theorem [[thm-hh-finite-dual-coalgebra-and-hopf-descent]] proves that this subset is a vector subspace and that the transposed multiplication $m_A^*(f)$, defined by $m_A^*(f)(a\otimes b)=f(ab)$, corestricts to $A^\circ\otimes A^\circ$. Let $k$ be a field.

1. Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $M$ a free $R$-module of finite rank $n$ with basis $(e_0,\dots,e_{n-1})$, and let $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}\in M$ span $M$. Then the coordinate matrix $A$ of $(v_0,\dots,v_{n-1})$ in the basis $(e_i)$ has a right inverse, $\det(A)$ is a unit of $R$, and $(v_0,\dots,v_{n-1})$ is a basis of $M$. The determinant is formed for $n\ge1$; for $n=0$ the module is the zero module and the empty family is its basis, with no determinant clause.
2. If $F\subseteq E$ is a field extension and $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, then the rank of $A$ over $F$ equals its rank over $E$.
3. Let $B$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-algebra and $N$ a finite-dimensional left $B$-module. A proper submodule has strictly smaller $k$-dimension, a maximal proper submodule of a nonzero finite-dimensional module exists by maximal dimension (no arbitrary Choice), and iterating produces a finite composition series of $N$ ([[def-composition-series-and-length-of-a-module]]); in particular $N$ has finite length.
4. If $S_1,\dots,S_m$ are simple $B$-modules and $N\subseteq S_1\oplus\cdots\oplus S_m$ is a submodule, then $N$ is isomorphic to a direct sum of a subfamily of the $S_i$, and $N$ has a complement in $S_1\oplus\cdots\oplus S_m$.
5. If $T:N\to N$ is $k$-linear with $T^r=0$ for some $r\ge1$, then $\operatorname{tr}(T)=0$ ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

For ordered bases $(v_1,\dots,v_m)$ of $V$, $(w_1,\dots,w_n)$ of $W$ with dual bases $(v_i^*)$, $(w_j^*)$, the image of $v_i^*\otimes w_j^*$ is the dual basis vector of $v_i\otimes w_j$ in the product basis of $V\otimes W$.

For every ordered basis $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ of $V$ the element $\sum_{i=1}^nv_i^*\otimes v_i\in V^*\otimes V$ is independent of the basis and corresponds to $\mathrm{id}_V$ under the isomorphism $V^*\otimes V\to\operatorname{Hom}(V,V)$, $f\otimes v\mapsto[x\mapsto f(x)v]$ ([[thm-hom-from-a-finite-dimensional-space-as-a-tensor-product]]). Fix a field $k$. Require $\Delta:H\to H\otimes H$ and $\varepsilon:H\to k$ to be unital algebra homomorphisms. The algebra on $H\otimes H$ is the one with $(a\otimes b)(c\otimes d)=ac\otimes bd$ and unit $1_H\otimes1_H$; the algebra on $k$ is its field algebra. A **bialgebra map** $f:H\to K$ is a $k$-linear map preserving multiplication, unit, comultiplication, and counit: $f m_H=m_K(f\otimes f)$, $fu_H=u_K$, $\Delta_Kf=(f\otimes f)\Delta_H$, and $\varepsilon_Kf=\varepsilon_H$.

$$S(ab)=S(b)S(a),\qquad \Delta(S(h))=(S\otimes S)\tau\Delta(h)\quad(h\in H),$$

where $\tau(x\otimes y)=y\otimes x$ is the tensor flip. In particular, these are consequences of the convolution-inverse definition; they are not extra axioms.

Let $f:M\to M'$ be a homomorphism of right $R$-modules and $g:N\to N'$ a homomorphism of left $R$-modules. There is a unique group homomorphism

$$f\otimes g:M\otimes_RN\longrightarrow M'\otimes_RN'$$

such that $(f\otimes g)(m\otimes n)=f(m)\otimes g(n)$. These maps satisfy

$$\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\operatorname{id}_N=\operatorname{id}_{M\otimes_RN}$$

and

$$(f'\circ f)\otimes(g'\circ g)=(f'\otimes g')\circ(f\otimes g).$$

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $A,B$ be $R$-algebras. The $R$-module $A\otimes_RB$ has a unique $R$-algebra structure satisfying

$$(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')=aa'\otimes bb'$$

and

$$1_{A\otimes_RB}=1_A\otimes1_B,\qquad r\longmapsto r(1_A\otimes1_B).$$

If $A$ and $B$ are commutative, then $A\otimes_RB$ is commutative.

derivations.claim: If $f\in A^\circ$ vanishes on a finite-codimensional two-sided ideal $I$, and $g\in A^\circ$ vanishes on such an ideal $J$, then $f,g$ and every linear combination vanish on $I\cap J$. The map $A/(I\cap J)\to A/I\oplus A/J$, $a+(I\cap J)\mapsto(a+I,a+J)$, is injective, so its image is a subspace of a finite-dimensional vector space and is finite-dimensional by [F2]. Thus $A^\circ$ is a vector subspace.

Let $q:A\to A/I$ be the quotient map and write $f=\bar f q$. Since $A/I$ is finite-dimensional, [F3] identifies $((A/I)\otimes(A/I))^*$ with $(A/I)^*\otimes(A/I)^*$; the transpose of multiplication on $A/I$ therefore gives a finite tensor $\sum_i\bar f_i\otimes\bar g_i$ with $\bar f(ab)=\sum_i\bar f_i(a+I)\bar g_i(b+I)$. Pulling the factors back along $q$ yields $\Delta^\circ(f)=\sum_i(\bar f_iq)\otimes(\bar g_iq)\in A^\circ\otimes A^\circ$, and its evaluation on $a\otimes b$ is $f(ab)$.

If $f(a)=\ell(\rho(a)v)$ is a coefficient of a finite-dimensional representation $\rho:A\to\operatorname{End}_k(V)$, then $\ker\rho$ is a two-sided ideal of finite codimension and $f(\ker\rho)=0$, so $f\in A^\circ$. Conversely, if $f$ vanishes on a finite-codimensional ideal $I$, the finite-dimensional quotient $V=A/I$ is a left $A$-module by $a\cdot(b+I)=ab+I$; the vector $v=1+I$ and functional $\ell(b+I)=f(b)$ are well-defined and satisfy $f(a)=\ell(a\cdot v)$. Thus the finite-dual functionals are exactly the finite-dimensional matrix coefficients.

The evaluation map $A^*\otimes A^*\to(A\otimes A)^*$ is injective: write a finite tensor as $\sum_{i=1}^r\phi_i\otimes\psi_i$ with the $\phi_i$ linearly independent, by choosing a basis of the finite span of its first factors and rewriting. The map $A\to k^r$, $a\mapsto(\phi_1(a),\dots,\phi_r(a))$, is surjective, since a proper subspace of the finite-dimensional space $k^r$ has a nonzero annihilating linear functional, which would give a nontrivial dependence among the $\phi_i$. Choose $a_j$ mapping to the $j$-th standard vector; if the tensor evaluates to zero on every $a\otimes b$, then $\psi_j(b)=0$ for every $b$ and every $j$, so the tensor is zero. Therefore the tensor characterized in step 1.2 is independent of the chosen ideal $I$.

For coefficients $f(a)=\ell(\rho(a)v)$ and $g(a)=\mu(\sigma(a)w)$ of finite-dimensional representations on $V,W$, define $(\rho\otimes\sigma)(a\otimes b)=\rho(a)\otimes\sigma(b)$. By [F6], this is well-defined; on pure tensors it preserves products because $(\rho(aa')\otimes\sigma(bb'))=(\rho(a)\rho(a')\otimes\sigma(b)\sigma(b'))=(\rho(a)\otimes\sigma(b))(\rho(a')\otimes\sigma(b'))$, and it preserves the unit. Composing with the unital algebra map $\Delta_H$ from [F4] gives a finite-dimensional unital representation. Its coefficient at $\ell\otimes\mu,v\otimes w$ is $\sum f(h_1)g(h_2)=(f*g)(h)$, so convolution preserves $H^\circ$.

If $f(a)=\ell(\rho(a)v)$, define an action on $V^*$ by $(h\cdot\lambda)(v')=\lambda(\rho(S_H(h))v')$. By [F5], $S_H(hh')=S_H(h')S_H(h)$, whence $(h\cdot(h'\cdot\lambda))(v')=\lambda(S_H(h')S_H(h)v')=((hh')\cdot\lambda)(v')$, and the unit acts as the identity. The coefficient of this finite-dimensional representation at vector $\ell\in V^*$ and functional $\operatorname{ev}_v(\lambda)=\lambda(v)$ is $f(S_H(h))$. Therefore $S_H^*(f)\in H^\circ$.

For $f\in A^\circ$, evaluation of $(\Delta^\circ\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta^\circ(f)$ and $(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta^\circ)\Delta^\circ(f)$ on $a\otimes b\otimes c$ gives $f((ab)c)$ and $f(a(bc))$, equal by associativity. The evaluation map on three finite tensor factors is injective by repeating the finite-independent-family argument of step 2.1. Evaluating $(\varepsilon^\circ\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta^\circ(f)$ and $(\mathrm{id}\otimes\varepsilon^\circ)\Delta^\circ(f)$ at $a$ gives $f(1_Aa)=f(a)=f(a1_A)$, so these maps are the identity.

The functional $\varepsilon_H$ lies in $H^\circ$: its kernel is a two-sided ideal, and the induced map $H/\ker\varepsilon_H\to k$ is injective by definition of the kernel and surjective since $\varepsilon_H(1_H)=1$. It is the convolution unit by the two counit equations for $H$. The coproduct $\Delta^\circ(f)$ is a finite tensor by step 1.2. For $f,g\in H^\circ$ and $a,b\in H$, $\Delta^\circ(f*g)(a\otimes b)=(f*g)(ab)=\sum f(a_1b_1)g(a_2b_2)=(\Delta^\circ(f)\Delta^\circ(g))(a\otimes b)$, because [F4] makes $\Delta_H$ an algebra map. By the tensor-evaluation injectivity of step 2.1, this proves coproduct multiplicativity. If $I=k[x]$, a functional vanishing on it is zero, which is the empty sum in the claimed direct sum.

The primitive coproduct sends a polynomial $p(x)$ to $p(X+Y)$ in $k[X,Y]$. Writing $X=a+u$, $Y=b+v$, the value of $(\delta_{a,r}*\delta_{b,s})(p)$ is the coefficient of $u^rv^s$ in $p(a+b+u+v)$. Expanding $p(a+b+z)=\sum_n\delta_{a+b,n}(p)z^n$, that coefficient is $\binom{r+s}{r}\delta_{a+b,r+s}(p)$; hence $\delta_{a,r}*\delta_{b,s}=\binom{r+s}{r}\delta_{a+b,r+s}$, with binomial coefficients interpreted in $k$.

For a proper cofinite ideal, $p$ has positive degree. Repeatedly applying [F1] and dividing by $x-a$ whenever $a$ is a root factors $p$, up to a nonzero scalar, as $\prod_{a\in E}(x-a)^{m_a}$ for a finite set $E\subset k$ of distinct roots and positive integers $m_a$. If $a\ne b$, then $u=(x-a)/(b-a)$ and $v=-(x-b)/(b-a)$ satisfy $u+v=1$, with $u\in(x-a)$ and $v\in(x-b)$. Expanding $1=(u+v)^{m+n-1}$ shows $(x-a)^m+(x-b)^n=k[x]$, since every term contains either at least $m$ factors $u$ or at least $n$ factors $v$. Pulling these functionals back to $k[x]$ expresses any $f$ vanishing on $(p)$ as a finite sum of $\delta_{a,r}$. For $f,g\in k[x]$, expand $f=\sum_i\delta_{a,i}(f)(x-a)^i$ and $g=\sum_j\delta_{a,j}(g)(x-a)^j$. The coefficient of $(x-a)^r$ in $fg$ is $\sum_{i+j=r}\delta_{a,i}(f)\delta_{a,j}(g)$; by [F5], this gives $\Delta^\circ\delta_{a,r}=\sum_{i+j=r}\delta_{a,i}\otimes\delta_{a,j}$.

Let $k$ be a field. Let $H$ be a Hopf $k$-algebra and $I\trianglelefteq H$ a Hopf ideal. The quotient $H/I$ has a unique Hopf structure making the quotient map $q:H\to H/I$ a Hopf map. Every Hopf map $f:H\to K$ that kills $I$ factors uniquely through $q$ as a Hopf map. For any Hopf map $f:H\to K$, its kernel is a Hopf ideal.

For Hopf $k$-algebras $H,K$, the tensor product $H\otimes K$ is a Hopf algebra with multiplication $m_{H\otimes K}=(m_H\otimes m_K)(\mathrm{id}_H\otimes\tau_{K,H}\otimes\mathrm{id}_K)$, coproduct $\Delta_{H\otimes K}=(\mathrm{id}_H\otimes\tau_{H,K}\otimes\mathrm{id}_K)(\Delta_H\otimes\Delta_K)$, unit $u_H\otimes u_K$, counit $\varepsilon_H\otimes\varepsilon_K$, and antipode $S_H\otimes S_K$, where $\tau$ flips the two middle tensor factors. The quotient and tensor-product constructions are choice-free. AC is assumed for the kernel assertion and is used only for tensor-kernel exactness over arbitrary vector spaces.

Let $k$ be any field.

1. For any group $G$, the vector space $kG$ of finite sums $\sum_{g\in G}a_g g$ is a Hopf algebra. Its multiplication is the bilinear extension of the group law, its unit is the group identity $e$, and
   $$\Delta(g)=g\otimes g,\qquad \varepsilon(g)=1,\qquad S(g)=g^{-1}\quad(g\in G).$$
2. For any finite group $G$, the pointwise algebra $k^G$ of all functions $f:G\to k$ is a Hopf algebra with
   $$\Delta(f)(x,y)=f(xy),\qquad \varepsilon(f)=f(e),\qquad S(f)(x)=f(x^{-1}).$$
   The finite-set tensor identification $k^G\otimes k^G\cong k^{G\times G}$ is used to define $\Delta$. No Hopf structure on the full function space $k^G$ for infinite $G$ is claimed.
3. The polynomial algebra $k[x]$ is a Hopf algebra with
   $$\Delta(x)=x\otimes1+1\otimes x,\qquad \varepsilon(x)=0,\qquad S(x)=-x.$$
   These formulas work in every characteristic. The element $x$ is primitive in every characteristic, and in characteristic $p>0$ so is $x^p$.

derivations.claim: Applying [F1] to these two Hopf algebras gives the tensor-product Hopf structure. The tensor algebra multiplication yields $(g\otimes x^i)(h\otimes x^j)=gh\otimes x^{i+j}$, and it also shows that $g\otimes1$ commutes with $1\otimes x$.

Since $\Delta(x)=1\otimes x+x\otimes1$ and the two summands commute in $k[x]\otimes k[x]$, the binomial theorem gives $\Delta(x^n)=\sum_{r=0}^n\binom nr x^r\otimes x^{n-r}$. Combining this with $\Delta(g)=g\otimes g$ and the flipped middle factors in [F1] gives the displayed formula for $\Delta(g\otimes x^n)$.

The tensor antipode in [F1] gives $S(g\otimes x^n)=g^{-1}\otimes(-x)^n$. Directly, for the left antipode product on a basis tensor, $\sum_{r=0}^n\binom nr(g^{-1}\otimes(-x)^r)(g\otimes x^{n-r}) =(1\otimes x^n)\sum_{r=0}^n\binom nr(-1)^r,$ which is $1\otimes1$ for $n=0$ and $0$ for $n>0$. The right product is $(1\otimes x^n)\sum_{r=0}^n\binom nr(-1)^{n-r}$, with the same values. Thus the explicit formulas agree with both antipode equations from [F1].

By [F1], the tensor-product counit is $\varepsilon_{kG}\otimes\varepsilon_{k[x]}$. The group-algebra counit has $\varepsilon_{kG}(g)=1$, while the polynomial counit is a unital algebra map with $\varepsilon_{k[x]}(x)=0$ by [F2], so it takes $1=x^0$ to $1$ and $x^n$ to $0$ for $n>0$. Therefore $\varepsilon(g\otimes x^n)=1$ for $n=0$ and $0$ for $n>0$, as claimed.
